title: Unit 1 Quiz · Problems, Algorithms and Problem Solving
instructions: 33 questions, 39 marks. You have 30 minutes; the quiz submits itself when time runs out.
Questions and options are shuffled, so your neighbour's screen will not match yours.
Multi-select questions need ALL correct options for the marks. Ordering questions give part marks for each item in the right place.
After submitting you will see your score and an explanation for every question.

questions.q: Which of these is a problem INSTANCE rather than a problem?
options: Find the largest of any n numbers
Decide whether a whole number n ≥ 2 is prime
Sort any list of names alphabetically
questions.explain: An instance has actual input values filled in (12, 47, 33). The other three describe every possible input, so they are problems.

questions.q: Why must a program be tested on more than the one example given in the question?
options: A program solves the whole problem, so it must work for every valid instance
Because the compiler needs at least two runs
Because one example always gives a wrong answer
It does not need to; one correct example proves it works
questions.explain: A problem has infinitely many instances. One correct example shows nothing about the others, especially special cases.
60 × 61 / 2 = 3660 / 2 = 1830. (3660 is what you get if you forget to divide by 2.)

questions.q: For the average-marks program, select ALL the inputs that are special cases worth testing.
questions.explain: n = 0 would divide by zero, n = 1 is the smallest valid input, 105 is out of range. A normal class is a typical case, not a special one.

questions.q: “Is 2028 a leap year?” is which type of problem?
questions.explain: The answer is yes or no, so it is a decision problem.

questions.q: “Find the shortest route that starts at college, visits 6 shops and returns” is which type of problem?
questions.explain: Many routes are valid; we want the best (shortest) one. That is an optimization problem.

questions.q: The halting problem (deciding, for every program, whether it will ever stop) is an example of:
options: An unsolvable problem: no algorithm can solve it for all inputs
A counting problem with a very large answer
A problem that only needs a faster computer
questions.explain: Alan Turing proved in 1936 that no algorithm can decide halting for every program. More speed does not help.

questions.q: Checking every round trip through n cities needs (n − 1)! / 2 routes. How many routes for 6 cities?
questions.explain: (6 − 1)! / 2 = 5! / 2 = 120 / 2 = 60. The count grows so fast that this problem is called intractable for large n.

questions.q: Which of these is an ILL-DEFINED problem?
options: Count the students with attendance below 75%
questions.explain: “Better” has no clear input, output or measure. It must be turned into precise questions before a computer can help.

questions.q: Request: “Write a program to calculate the electricity bill.” Which question is LEAST useful to ask?
options: What is the rate per unit, and does it change after a certain number of units?
Is there a fixed monthly charge?
Can units consumed be a decimal number?
What brand of meter is used?
questions.explain: A good question is one whose answer changes the program. The meter brand does not affect the calculation.

questions.q: Arrange Pólya’s problem-solving steps in the correct order.
questions.explain: Understand → Plan → Execute → Review. Review often sends you back to understand the problem better.

questions.q: Before coding, you work out by hand that marks 72, 85, 64 should give 73.67. This belongs mainly to which step?
questions.explain: Solving a small instance by hand is how you make sure you understand what is asked. The result is reused later to check the program in Review.

questions.q: Splitting “print a report card” into read marks, validate, calculate and print is called:
questions.explain: Breaking a big problem into smaller subproblems, then refining each, is top-down decomposition (stepwise refinement).

questions.q: A complete specification of the input “marks” should state:
options: Its name, type, valid range and unit (e.g. integer 0–100, out of 100)
Only how the output will look
questions.explain: Name, type, range and unit together remove doubt. Without the range, nobody knows if 105 or −5 is acceptable.

questions.q: Attendance is entered as 112%. Which validation check rejects it?
questions.explain: 112 is a number (type is fine) but it is outside 0–100. That is a range check.

questions.q: Select ALL of the following that are kinds of input validation.
questions.explain: Type, range and presence checks examine the user’s input. Compiling checks the program’s code, not the input.

questions.q: What is the pre-condition of binary search?
options: The list must have an even number of items
The key must be in the list
The list must have fewer than 1000 items
questions.explain: Binary search throws away half the list based on order. On an unsorted list it can miss the key. The key does not have to be present: then it reports “not found”.

questions.q: For an algorithm that computes the square root r of x, which is the PRE-condition?
questions.explain: The pre-condition is about the input before the algorithm runs: x ≥ 0. The others describe the result, so they are post-conditions.

questions.q: A recipe step says “add salt to taste”. Which property of an algorithm does it violate?
questions.explain: Definiteness means every step is exact and unambiguous. “To taste” means different things to different people.

questions.q: Select ALL the properties that every algorithm must have.
options: Finiteness: it stops after a finite number of steps
Effectiveness: every step is basic enough to do by hand
It must be written in C
questions.explain: Knuth’s properties are finiteness, definiteness, input (zero or more), output (at least one) and effectiveness. An algorithm is independent of any programming language.

questions.q: You pay ₹289 greedily (largest first) with notes/coins of 200, 50, 20, 10, 5, 2 and 1. How many pieces do you use?
Binary search is an example of which solution approach?
questions.explain: Each comparison splits the remaining list in half and continues with one half: divide and conquer.

questions.q: Linear search on a list of 1,000 items: how many comparisons in the WORST case?
questions.explain: Worst case: the key is last or not present, so all 1,000 items are checked. Best case is 1; average about (n + 1) / 2 ≈ 500.

questions.q: Binary search on a sorted list of 10,00,000 roll numbers needs AT MOST about how many comparisons?
questions.explain: Each comparison halves the range. 2²⁰ = 10,48,576 ≥ 10,00,000, so about 20 comparisons (log₂ n).

questions.q: Arrange these growth rates from SLOWEST-growing to FASTEST-growing.
questions.explain: 1 < log n < n < n log n < n² < 2ⁿ for large n. At n = 10⁶ these are about 1, 20, 10⁶, 2 × 10⁷ and 10¹² steps; 2ⁿ is astronomically larger.

questions.q: To check whether 10,007 (a prime) is prime, you try divisors only from 2 up to √n. About how many divisions is that?
questions.explain: √10,007 ≈ 100, so divisors 2 … 100: 99 divisions. Trying all of 2 … n − 1 would need 10,005.

questions.q: How many times does the statement sum = sum + i run when n = 50?
questions.explain: The loop runs once for each i from 1 to 50: 50 additions. (1275 is the final value of sum, not the number of steps.)

questions.q: An algorithm is TOTALLY correct when:
options: It always stops, and when it stops the answer is right
It gives the right answer for the example in the question
It runs in less than one second
questions.explain: Total correctness = partial correctness (right answer if it stops) + termination (it always stops).

questions.q: For the loop below, which statement is true after every pass i (a loop invariant)?
questions.explain: After pass i the loop has added 1 to i, so sum = 1 + … + i. When the loop ends (i = n) this becomes the post-condition sum = n(n + 1)/2.

questions.q: Grades: 80–100 A, 60–79 B, … , valid marks 0–100. Which set of inputs best tests the BOUNDARIES of grade A?
questions.explain: Boundary-value testing checks both sides of each edge of grade A: 79/80 and 100/101.

questions.q: This code should give A for 80–100. Which input exposes the bug?
questions.explain: The condition should be marks >= 80. With > 80, the boundary value 80 wrongly gets B. 79 gets B correctly.

questions.q: Which of these can NOT be computed with just a running total and a count, and needs every mark stored (e.g. in an array)?
questions.explain: The median is the middle value after sorting, so all marks must be kept. Average, total and count only need a few variables.

questions.q: Print requests are served first come, first served. Which data structure fits best?
questions.explain: First in, first out is a queue. A stack is last in, first out (like Undo).
